Game Interfaces

  • Games contain four main components: decisions, oppositions, rules, and goals.
  • Players, however, will only see the game interface.
  • The objective of designing games is to combine these components through an interface in order to communicate information to the player.

Game Development: Designers & Artists

  • Game developers will have to work alongside art designers (who create the UI/UX design)
  • It is important not to undermine the art designers behind a game interface.

User Interfaces

  • The user interface consists of all the visual elements of the game. This includes the game state, the player actions, and state changes.
  • The goal of a user interface is to convey this information to users, in addition to formal element-based information such as the game rules, player inventories, etc.

Mapping Code to User Experiences

Goal of a User Interface
A basic example of some backend game code has been provided below

class Hero {
	int health;
	int max_health;
};

class MovementAI {
	int[] MovementParameters;
	Behaviour abcde;
}

// (...)

While this code makes sense to developers, it is meaningless to users unless the elements shown have been implemented into a functional AI that allows the player to interact with the parameters shown.

The User Interface allows us to communicate game concepts and principles to the mind of the user.

(Code example)...

health = 127;
max_health = 140;

// We need to display this visually....

... (to visual example)

We need to communicate the current game state to the user in as simple a form as possible.

User Interface Elements

Different interface elements will serve different purposes.

For example, Minecraft allows you to access crafting tables/furnaces via an on-screen GUI.

The display will also show the player's hotbar inventory at the bottom of the screen.

Both of these are interface elements, but both will serve a different part of the game's backend and provide a different purpose to the user.

UI Element Types: 3 Ways To Display Information

  • Heads-Up Display [HUD)]
    Refers to any transparent display that presents data to a user - where the user does not need to look away from their standard viewpoints.

  • Menus
    A more traditional way of displaying information. Unlike an HUD, players may have to interact with an icon to access the information.

  • Icons
    Another way to display information, often for simpler data.

UI vs UX

UI (User Interface) Designers will create the elements that users will act on when playing the game. This includes hotbars, HUDs, menus, icons, etc.

UX (User eXperience) Designers, on the other hand, will design the game's physical layout and structure. They will determine where elements should be positioned spatially.

UX is the entire information architecture of a game.

UI and UX Difference Example

A UI designer may ask the question 'how can I make the health bar stand out more?'
This could include changing the colours, etc.
Whereas a UX designer may ask the question 'where can this health bar be positioned so that it doesn't block the player's view?'
This could include making the element smaller, only placing it in the top left, etc.

  • UX design is heavily dependent on the target audience and target platform.
  • For example, audiences that read right-to-left may prefer their elements on the right of the screen.
  • Positioning of elements for mobile devices is very different to desktops.

UI/UX Timeframe
UX design will often take place before UI design. The UI will be built on top of the UX.

UX designers will need some knowledge of coding, whereas UI designers are better with a background in art/creativity.

UI/UX Visual Design Principles

Recognizing Diversity
Effective UIs and UXs will account for differences in platform, and allow many types of players to intuitively understand/act upon the information presented to them. This could mean, for example, that the game accounts for children and adults, or non-western and western audiences, etc.

Game Genres
Different game genres will require different levels of robustness to the provided UI. The importance and role of a UI will vary per game.
